prize_parts.citation: For the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, made possible by the conception, construction and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments.

statement.case_for: The observation of the Higgs boson is the clearest case on the list of nature supplying the decisive clue: a particle predicted in 1964 was found in 2012 by two independent detectors, completing the Standard Model and confirming electroweak symmetry breaking. The 2013 prize honoured the theory, so the discovery itself remains unrecognised. Coupling and mass measurements over more than a decade are consistent with the Standard Model, so maturity is not in question. Mehlig, Pearce, Olsson and Eriksson all rank it, and nobody disputes the science; the only real obstacle is attribution, and that is a problem of how to credit, not of whether the discovery deserves it. Honouring the conception and leadership of the two experiments, in a form that names both ATLAS and CMS, is a defensible way to do that.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a prize to three people cannot fairly represent two collaborations of thousands, and leadership roles at conception or announcement are not the same as scientific authorship of the discovery. The trio will inevitably exclude Virdee, whose CMS role is comparable to Della Negra's, and the choice among Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee is partly arbitrary. The committee could also conclude that the 2013 award already covered the discovery, or that a prize which is mostly institutional leadership is a worse use of the prize than a case with clean individual credit such as magic-angle graphene (B041) or optical lattices (B001). I take this seriously and do not consider the attribution problem resolved.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Higgs discovery highly on importance and maturity but worries that leadership rather than specific scientific contribution is being rewarded, and that CMS is thinly represented in the Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni trio.
responses.response: I agree the leadership-versus-contribution worry is real, and I do not think it can be fully answered. But for detector-driven discoveries the conception and construction of an instrument able to find a particle in huge backgrounds is the scientific contribution, and the two experiments' founding leaders are the people whose decisions made the search possible. On balance, a 2:1 split between ATLAS and CMS is a consequence of the three-person cap. Swapping Jenni for Virdee would only tilt the imbalance the other way. I would accept a CMS-weighted trio if the committee preferred it, but I do not see a configuration that avoids the problem.

responses.point: Eriksson puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first: a simple continuum-model prediction followed by an experiment, spawning a broad moire field, while acknowledging that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and that first-author experimentalists are not credited.
responses.response: I share Eriksson's admiration for the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and I ranked B041 third myself, so this is a difference of judgement, not of principle. My hesitation is maturity. Eight years after the experiments the superconducting mechanism is still debated, and Eriksson himself notes the uncredited junior experimentalists and the sample dependence. The Higgs result has no such open question about what was discovered. I would not oppose B041 in a later year, and it is my first alternative, but I do not think it is yet the stronger case.

responses.point: Pearce, as an instrumentalist, ranks the Higgs first and proposes Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as the founding ATLAS and CMS leaders, treating Gianotti as a defensible alternative because she led ATLAS at the announcement.
responses.response: I agree with the reasoning about detector conception, and with Pearce that this is where the strongest claim lies. Where I differ is in including Gianotti rather than Virdee. Her role at the time of the discovery, as ATLAS spokesperson, is the most visible link to the 2012 result, whereas Virdee's claim rests mainly on CMS project leadership. That is a close call, and I would not make it a point of principle. It does show that the choice between the four names cannot be settled from the file alone, and I would like the chair to push on it in the next round.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B011 first, the Cirac-Zoller theory proposals, and argues that the optical-lattice experiments are better kept separate so that the same people are not rewarded twice.
responses.response: The overlap argument is fair, and it is why I propose only the experimental trio for B001 when I rank it, rather than a mixed configuration. But a prize to theory alone, however original, is a weaker fit with the experimental record the committee usually rewards. B011 also has support from only two members. I would be willing to look at B001 with a theory component, but I would not put B011 ahead of the Higgs discovery.

uncertainties: Which three of the four credited names (Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) best represent ATLAS and CMS, and whether leadership roles can ground a prize at all.
Whether the committee sees the experimental discovery as sufficiently distinct from the 2013 prize, and whether a separate accelerator or detector-construction entry should be preferred.
Whether the pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene is settled enough for B041 to overtake the Higgs discovery on maturity.
For B001, whether the prize should be experimental, theoretical or mixed, and how to choose among five credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) are not linked to any shortlisted candidate, and my own research is in string theory and cosmology, so I rely on the supplied evidence for all candidates.
